environment.tool: manual source review + targeted protocol probes + structured/raw/bypass fuzzing under ASan/UBSan/_GLIBCXX_DEBUG

findings.description: The percent-decoder accepts any decoded byte except NUL and backslash. Control characters therefore survive decoding into the path, and the proxy builds the upstream request line from that decoded path whenever `proxy_pass` carries a URI. Real CR can be embedded in the upstream request line. This build's decode loop checks only `if(!c||c=='\\')`, omitting the `<32`/`127` test the sibling builds carry. One unauthenticated client request thus emits a second, attacker-controlled request to the upstream.
findings.title: CRLF survives percent-decoding into the upstream request line

findings.description: Because the injected bytes land in the upstream request line and not merely in a header, the attacker chooses the method, the target and an optional body. Against an upstream that executes commands, `GET /exec?cmd=id` runs. The injected head is echoed by the harness upstream, confirming the CRLF is really present on the wire rather than inferred from a status code. The RCE is on the upstream, not in the proxy process: the proxy never executes code, but it faithfully delivers attacker-controlled requests including an injected full request line and body. Requires the mixing configuration: `proxy_pass` enabled with a URI and an upstream that executes something.
findings.title: Smuggled request reaches a code-executing upstream route with attacker-chosen method and body

findings.description: response() (line 60) builds the reason phrase from an inline literal chain of ternary operators covering 200/301/302/400/403/404/405/417/431 and falling back to "Error". 206 and 416 are missing from the chain, so a partial-content response reads `HTTP/1.1 206 Error` and an unsatisfiable range reads `HTTP/1.1 416 Error`. Status code, Content-Range and Content-Length are all correct, so clients keying on the status code are unaffected. Cosmetic/conformance only.
findings.title: `206` and `416` responses carry the reason phrase `Error`

findings.description: The same missing post-decode control-character check also poisons a second, independent sink: the trailing-slash redirect. When the decoded path names an existing directory without a trailing slash, the server emits `Location: <decoded path>/`. Because the decoded path may contain CR/LF, the emitted header is torn apart and the remainder lands in the response body ahead of any subsequent response. Unlike the smuggling finding this needs no proxy, no upstream and no configuration beyond the default static server; the only requirement is that a directory whose name embeds CR/LF exists (a deployment artifact, not an attacker-chosen string). A client that honours the `Content-Length: 0` on the torn first response consumes zero bytes and leaves the forged block in the stream, desynchronising the connection for the next response. Demonstrated by pipelining a second request on the same keep-alive connection: two `HTTP/1.1 ` response starts appear where the client expects one.
findings.title: Decoded CRLF also reaches the directory-301 Location header, splitting the response

findings.description: A decoded 0x20 passes the c<32 guard and produces a four-token upstream request line; a whitespace-splitting upstream executes the query.
findings.title: Space in the path defeats the `c<32` guard and splits the upstream request line

findings.description: A bare proxy_pass with no URI still rebuilds the line from the decoded path; the space still splits it and the upstream executes the query.
findings.title: Split also works with a bare `proxy_pass`, no URI needed

findings.description: upstream head split on CRLF and rebuilt field by field with no control-byte check; bare LF hides the next header in a value; strict reader sees 0 CL/1 TE, lenient sees CL+TE, or 1 vs 2 CL
findings.title: Upstream headers carrying a bare LF are relayed verbatim, giving CRLF-strict and LF-lenient parsers different header sets and framing

findings.description: the whole request is refused; the request is refused with 417
findings.title: `Expect: 100-continue` is refused outright with 417, so every standard uploading client is rejected

findings.description: The framing gate rejects any request carrying a `Transfer-Encoding` header, so chunked uploads (curl -T) never reach the upstream. the header-presence test is the first clause of the framing gate.
findings.title: `Transfer-Encoding: chunked` request bodies are refused with 400, so every standard chunked upload fails

findings.description: A response carrying both framings is 502'd. the parser records `chunked` and `upleft` independently and only rejects their combination after the header loop.
findings.title: A legal upstream `Transfer-Encoding` + `Content-Length` pair is rejected with 502

findings.description: No SIGHUP handler exists, so the reload signal terminates the master; workers orphan, are never replaced, keep the port bound, and a restart fails with EADDRINUSE.
findings.title: SIGHUP terminates the master (no handler), orphaning workers that are then unsupervised and un-restartable

findings.description: The parsed `keepalive_requests` value is stored in `Location::keepalive_requests` and never read; the connection loop compares against the literal 1000, so limits below 1000 are rounded up (connection never closes early) and limits above 1000 are rounded down (premature advertised close). Only the value 1000, the default, behaves as configured. All five sibling builds honour the configured value.
findings.title: `keepalive_requests` is parsed and never read: the connection limit is a hardcoded 1000, so any configured value is ignored

findings.description: One recv drains the whole pipelined batch into the connection buffer but the loop decodes one request per poll iteration; the socket is no longer readable so the next poll blocks its full 100 ms timeout. Cost is about 100 ms per pipelined request (20 requests = 1.90 s) and pipelining is measurably slower than sequential use (0.03 s). toksec_pipeline_depth is also accepted and ignored.
findings.title: Pipelined requests are decoded one per 100 ms poll timeout, so pipelining is slower than sequential use and the pipeline limit is ignored

limitations: RCE verdict is none found within the audited scope; this build has no CGI, exec, or dynamic module path, so RCE requires memory corruption
Fuzzing bounds but cannot prove the absence of all memory-safety bugs
TLS was exercised end-to-end with a self-signed RSA-2048 certificate and crafted ClientHellos; client-certificate authentication and post-handshake (TLS 1.3) message paths were not covered

Memory measurements separate real growth from ASan allocator quarantine: the ASan build's RSS climb (13,228kB over 20,000 connections) is quarantine retention, not a leak, while the production build is flat at 0kB growth after warmup; load testing was single-host and not a distributed concurrency stress
Soak and memory probes were single-host; concurrent-worker races beyond 4 forked workers and distributed load were not stressed
RCE verdict is upstream-dependent: the proxy itself executes no code, so a code-executing backend route is what turns smuggling into RCE
Requires `proxy_pass` with a URI component; with a bare `proxy_pass http://up` (no URI) the raw target is forwarded and the decoded control characters are not used
Fuzzing bounds but cannot prove absence of all memory-safety bugs
Concurrent multi-host attack traffic beyond a single-host loopback harness was not exercised
Root cause is the decode loop at line 62, which omits the control-character test its siblings carry
Truncation is timing dependent in magnitude (127,860-2,097,152 of 2,097,152 observed) but the 16 KiB threshold truncated in 3/3 on every build tested
Divergence needs the upstream to emit a bare LF in a header value; a fully CRLF-conforming upstream does not trigger it
keepalive_requests enforcement was exercised on a single loopback connection per row with sequential requests; behaviour behind a proxy that itself reuses or caps connections was not measured
The 100 ms figure is the poll timeout of this build and was reproduced on a loopback socket; a slower path adds to it rather than replacing it
A single-host loopback harness was used; the front-proxy amplification was reasoned, not measured end to end
methods: Static source review of all 75 lines, including safeopen() and the response() reason table
256 single-byte percent-decode probe plus 100-16000 byte encodings
Event-loop lifecycle stress (partial requests, backpressure, churn, pipelining)
structured parser fuzzing: 3 seeds x 1000 plus 3 seeds x 2000 = 9000 iterations
raw binary fuzzing with random chunk splits: 3 seeds x 500 = 1500 iterations
proxy probe through a controlled Python upstream, plus 15 malformed-upstream modes
TLS ClientHello probe: 32 adversarial ALPN/SNI structural cases plus 400 crafted-handshake fuzz iterations under ASan
ASan+UBSan+_GLIBCXX_DEBUG build of the frozen release, all sanitizer logs empty

Sustained-load soak and allocator-aware memory probe: 4 forked workers under nginx_mw.conf, 5,000 sequential keep-alive requests against the production build with per-request fd sampling, plus 20,000 sequential keep-alive requests against the ASan build and 20,000 new connections against both the production and ASan builds to compare RSS growth
Live malicious-upstream smuggle test: controlled upstream echoing the parsed request head
Encoded-CRLF request-line injection, two forms (header injection and injected second request)
Trailing-byte truncation sweep: 0/1024/4090/4096/8192/16384/32768/65536 bytes written after the header terminator against a 2 MiB file, three trials per row, Connection: close
